overview.body:
**Raijin** ​(*raijin*) ‌— Thunder, ‌Lightning ​— ​belongs to ​the ​Japanese ​tradition. The ‌name ​means ​"Thunder god"[^1].

‌Raijin ​is ‌the personification ​of ‌thunder ​and lightning, ​one ​of ​the most ​dramatic ‌figures ​in ‌Japanese Buddhist ​and ‌folk ​art.

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the ‌name as ​**Raijin**. ​The ‌plain ASCII ‌form ‌*raijin* ​is the ​modern ‌Hepburn ​romanization; the ​restoration ‌capitalizes ​the conventional ​spelling. ‌Because ​the ‌Japanese source ​script ​uses ​logographic characters ​whose ‌distinctive ‌visual form ​cannot ‌be ​conveyed in ​the ‌basic ‌Latin alphabet, ‌and ‌because ​no diacritic ‌or ​special ​letter is ​added ‌in ​this ​restoration, the ​name ‌is ​placed in ​Tier ​2. ‌The Unicode ​form ‌remains ​the philologically ‌complete ​reference, ‌while the ‌ASCII ​spelling ​is a ​practical ​convenience ‌for the ‌domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Japanese characters ​as **雷神**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Thunder ​god"[^1].

Raijin ​means "thunder ‌god," from ​*rai* ​(thunder) and ‌*jin* (god, ​from Chinese ‌*shén*). He ​is the ‌Japanese personification ​of thunder ​and lightning, ​usually depicted ​as ​a red ‌demon beating ​drums to ‌produce thunder. ​His companion ‌is Fūjin, ​the wind ‌god.

The ​ASCII ‌form *raijin* ​survives only ​because the ‌early domain-name ‌system could ‌not carry ​Japanese characters ​or diacritics; ‌it is ​a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ​ancient spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration **Raijin** ​gives the ‌conventional Hepburn ​romanization with ​initial capitalization, ​the ​standard scholarly ‌way to ‌cite a ​proper name ‌in romanized ​Japanese. The ​name is ‌Tier 2 ‌because the ‌restoration ‌does not ​add a ‌distinctive diacritic ​or special ​letter absent ​from the ‌ASCII form.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**r** → ​**R** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **a** ‌→ **a** ​— Same
‌- **i** ​→ **i** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**j** → ‌**j** — ​Same
- ​**i** → ​**i** — ​Same
- ‌**n** → ‌**n** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/ɾa.i.dʑiɴ/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'RAIJIN' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Raijin ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*raijin* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Raijin** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Raijin** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*raijin* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Raijin ​governs thunder, ‌lightning, storms, ‌and ​the fearsome ​power ​of the ​sky. He ​is ‌both dangerous ​and ​protective: his ‌lightning can ​destroy, ‌but it ​can ‌also purify ​and ward ​off ​demons. In ​popular ​belief he ‌is associated ​with ‌the *Raijū*, ​a ‌creature that ​rides the ‌lightning.

​The domain ‌of ​**Raijin** is ​understood within ‌the ‌broader Japanese ‌religious ​landscape as ​both a ‌specific ​functional sphere ​and ‌a node ​in a ​network ‌of kami, ​buddhas, ‌and local ​spirits. Shrines, ​temples, ​and household ​rites ‌all invoke ‌the figure ​in ‌ways that ​blur ​strict boundaries ‌between Shinto ‌and ‌Buddhist practice[^3]. ‌The ​restoration **Raijin** ‌therefore names ​not ​only a ​mythic ‌person but ​a living ​field ​of ritual ‌activity: ​pilgrimage, festival, ​iconography, and ​prayer ‌continue to ​define ‌what the ​name means ‌in ​contemporary Japan. ‌This ‌combinatory or ​"syncretic" context ​is ​essential for ​interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
Raijin ​appears in ‌Japanese art ‌and folklore ​rather than ​as a ​central ​figure in ​the *Kojiki* ‌narrative. He ​is one ​of the ‌*kaminari-sama* ​whose thunder ‌is both ​a warning ‌and a ​punishment. The ​*Nihon ​Shoki* and ​later chronicles ​record thunder ‌deities associated ​with ‌specific mountains ​and storms. ‌In popular ​tales Raijin ‌is said ​to ‌eat children's ​navels, a ​fear parents ‌warded off ‌by hiding ‌their ​bellies during ​thunderstorms.

The ‌narrative of ​**Raijin** participates ​in the ‌larger ​mythic program ​of the ‌*Kojiki* and ​*Nihon Shoki*: ‌to explain ​the ​origins of ​the imperial ​house, the ‌division of ‌divine labour, ​and ‌the relationship ​between the ​human and ‌kami worlds. ‌Because these ‌chronicles ‌were compiled ​in the ‌eighth century ​under imperial ​patronage, the ​myths ‌also serve ​a political ​theology, grounding ​earthly authority ‌in ​divine descent ​and cosmic ​order[^3]. Read ‌comparatively, the ​story of ‌raijin ​illustrates how ‌Japanese myth ​uses genealogy, ‌descent from ‌heaven, and ​the ​negotiation of ​rival domains ​to construct ‌a coherent ‌sacred history.
​

cultural-legacy.body:
Raijin ​remains ‌a ‌staple of ​Japanese ​popular ​culture, ​from ​temple sculptures ‌and ​festival ​floats ‌to ​anime ‌and video ​games. ‌His ​fierce ​image ​represents the ​awe-inspiring ​side ‌of ​nature ‌and ​the protective ‌power ​that ‌guards ​sacred ‌space.

Today ​**Raijin** ​continues ‌to ‌appear ‌in ​shrine pilgrimage, ​festival ‌observance, ​anime, ​manga, ‌video games, ​and ​scholarly ‌discourse. ​The ‌name ​functions as ​both ​a ​religious ‌referent ‌and a ​cultural ‌symbol, ​a ​flexibility ‌that ‌has allowed ‌it ‌to ​survive ‌the ​formal separation ​of ​Shinto ‌and ​Buddhism ​and ​the secularisation ‌of ​modern ​Japan[^3]. ​Restoring ‌the conventional ​Hepburn ‌romanization ​keeps ‌the ​scholarly ‌citation intact ‌while ​acknowledging ​the ​living ​diversity of ‌its ‌meanings.
​

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are ​the earliest ​written witnesses ​to **Raijin**, ​although ​the figure ‌may have ​circulated ​in oral ‌and local ​cult forms ‌long ​before the ‌eighth century. ​In ​the chronicles, ​Raijin appears ​as ​the terrifying ‌drum-beating kami ​of storms, ‌often ​paired with ‌Fūjin the ​wind ‌god, embedded ​in the ‌imperial ​genealogy and ​the narrative ‌of cosmic ‌order[^1]. ‌The *Kojiki* ​account tends ​to ‌privilege the ​mythic lineage ​leading to ‌Amaterasu ​and the ​imperial house, ‌while ​the *Nihon ‌Shoki* often ​presents ​variant traditions ​side by ​side, preserving ‌conflicting ‌genealogies and ​episodes.

Because ‌both ​texts were ​compiled under ‌imperial patronage, ‌their ‌portrayal of ‌Raijin is ​never ‌purely "mythological" ​in a ​neutral ​sense; it ‌is also ​a statement ​about ​legitimacy, territory, ‌and the ​proper ​ordering of ​the human ‌and ​divine worlds[^2]. ‌Modern readers ​must therefore ‌distinguish ​between the ‌older narrative ‌strata ​preserved in ​the chronicles ​and the ​ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

shinto-sources.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Raijin** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Raijin ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Raijin ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Raijin** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Raijin ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Raijin through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
